title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Introduction
Clustering is a central technique in unsupervised machine learning, designed to reveal natural groupings within complex datasets where class labels are unknown. Among its methods, K-Means clustering remains widely applied for its simplicity, scalability, and interpretability (Mohd Talib, Abd Majid, and Sahran 2023). The algorithm partitions data into k groups based on similarity, minimizing within-cluster variance while maximizing between-cluster separation. This structure is valuable when the goal is understanding rather than prediction, such as comparing institutions by quantitative indicators of performance, resources, and access.
In higher education research, cluster analysis has long been used to explore structural and performance diversity across institutions (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005). This approach enables analyses that move beyond categorical labels and examine measurable dimensions such as outcomes, funding, and enrollment scale. A two-stage framework that combines factor analysis with clustering has also been proposed to derive empirically grounded institutional types (Elam 2016).
Standardized data and documentation have increased the reliability of these methods (National Center for Education Statistics 2023). Best practices for merging and cleaning educational datasets emphasize reproducibility and schema consistency in large-scale analysis (Kelchen 2019). Together, these sources point to the value of structured, data-driven methods in institutional research. The Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS), maintained by the National Center for Education Statistics, provides the standardized foundation for this type of large-scale institutional analysis. IPEDS collects consistent and comparable data on U.S. colleges and universities, making it a central source for empirical studies that analyze institutional differences through quantitative modeling.
Hybrid models further advance peer identification by pairing quantitative clustering with expert validation, improving interpretability and practical use (Texas Association for Institutional Research 2022). This balance between algorithmic precision and contextual review supports robust benchmarking and decision-making.
The present study applies K-Means clustering to IPEDS data to identify data-driven groupings of postsecondary institutions based on financial, academic, and outcome indicators. The objective is to uncover underlying institutional profiles that describe how U.S. colleges and universities align or differ in measurable ways, offering a transparent and scalable framework for understanding institutional diversity (Huberty, Jordan, and Brandt 2005; National Center for Education Statistics 2023; Elam 2016).

title: Literature Review
text:
1) Grocery stores in Kenya (customer segmentation)
Title: Application of K-Means Clustering for Customer Segmentation in Grocery Stores in Kenya
Link: https://ijstm.inarah.co.id/index.php/ijstm/article/view/1024
Summary:
This study groups grocery shoppers using K Means on transaction and basic demographic data. It matters because smaller stores still need simple ways to understand buying patterns and target customers better. The authors cleaned the data, tested cluster counts with the elbow method, and profiled the groups by behavior. The results gave clear segments that stores can use for marketing and stocking, though the setup is limited by the data available to small shops.

title: Literature Review
text:
2) Department store case (user profiling)
Title: Applying K-Means Clustering for User Profiling in Retail: A Department Store Case Study
Link: https://www.atlantis-press.com/article/125992628.pdf
Summary:
This paper uses membership and transaction data from a department store to build shopper profiles with K Means. It’s important because simple, interpretable clusters help teams design targeted offers and loyalty programs. The authors picked the number of clusters using the elbow method and the Calinski–Harabasz index, then described each group in plain terms. It shows a straightforward pipeline from retail data to actionable profiles, but it does not bring in extra context like demographics.

title: Literature Review
section: 3) Online retail with weighted K Means (RFM)
text:
3) Online retail with weighted K Means (RFM)
Title: Customer analytics for online retailers using weighted K-Means and RFM analysis
Link: https://pdfs.semanticscholar.org/2094/679b670242e4177670b839fd7736fc454afa.pdf
Summary:
This study tries to improve customer segmentation by combining RFM features (recency, frequency, monetary) with a weighted K Means variant. The goal is cleaner groups that help with targeting and retention. Using a large UK online retail dataset, the authors built RFM, compared standard vs weighted K Means, and evaluated with silhouette scores. Weighted K Means did better (about 0.40 vs 0.30), but using only RFM can miss other behavior, so the view of the customer is still limited.

title: Literature Review
section: 4) Comparing clustering algorithms on UK retail data
text:
4) Comparing clustering algorithms on UK retail data
Title: An Exploration of Clustering Algorithms for Customer Segmentation in the UK Retail Market
Link: https://arxiv.org/pdf/2402.04103
Summary:
This paper compares several clustering methods for retail segmentation using RFM features, including K Means, Gaussian Mixture Models, DBSCAN, BIRCH, and agglomerative clustering. It matters because the choice of algorithm changes how useful the groups are for marketing and planning. The results showed GMM scored highest on silhouette (around 0.80) in this setup, with K Means and others lower. The dataset is mostly transactions, so the clusters do not include extra context like demographics or browsing.

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Analysis and Results

Data Description and Visualization

Dataset Overview
This study uses institutional-level data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) for the 2023 collection year (2023–2024 cycle). IPEDS collects standardized information from all U.S. postsecondary institutions participating in federal financial aid programs, covering public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit sectors.
The following survey components were used and merged on the key UNITID:

HD2023 — Institutional characteristics (name, control, sector, etc.)
F2223_F1A — Finance (public, GASB)
F2223_F2 — Finance (private nonprofit, FASB)
F2223_F3 — Finance (private for-profit)
EFIA2023 — 12-month instructional activity (source of FTE)
ADM2023 — Admissions (admission rate, tuition; optional in analysis)
OM2023 — Outcome measures (completion/attainment; optional in analysis)

All files were downloaded from the NCES IPEDS Data Center.



Variable Selection and Preparation
To represent institutional scale, financial capacity, access, and outcomes, variables were drawn from multiple components and aligned by UNITID. Below are the primary fields used in this phase:








Feature Group
Variable (Field)
Description




Institutional Scale
FTE_TOTAL (built from EFIA2023)
Total full-time-equivalent enrollment (UG + Grad + DPP if present).


Financial Resources
TOT_REV (F1D01 / F2D162 / F3D12)
Total revenues (public), total revenues & investment return (nonprofit/for-profit).



INSTR_EXP (F1C011 / F2E011 / F3E011)
Instructional expenses (aligned across control types).



TOT_EXP (F1N07 / F2B02 / F3B02)
Total operating expenses.


Access & Price
e.g., ADM_RATE, TUITION1 (ADM2023)
Admission rate; in-state tuition/fees (if used).


Outcomes
e.g., OM2_PCT_COMP (OM2023)
8-year outcome/completion measure (if used).




Note: Where variables differ by control type, fields were harmonized to a shared name (e.g., TOT_REV, INSTR_EXP, TOT_EXP). Ratios per FTE are derived after FTE merge.




Data Cleaning and Integration
Finance data from public (F1A), private nonprofit (F2), and private for-profit (F3) files were imported and standardized to total revenue, instructional expense, and total expense. Twelve-month instructional activity (EFIA2023) provided undergraduate, graduate, and total FTE values; reported FTE were preferred, with estimated values as fallback.
Tables were merged using left joins on UNITID to preserve coverage. Numeric missing values were left as NA to maintain fidelity with NCES reporting. After filtering to active, degree-granting institutions with valid FTE, the analytic file contains ~6,000 institutions across all three control types.


Code
# ----libraries-------------------------------------------------------------
library(tidyverse)   # Data wrangling/joins/plots
library(janitor)     # Clean column names
library(gt)          # Summary tables
library(scales)      # Formatting
library(GGally)      # Quick pair plots
library(corrr)       # Correlation summaries
library(here)        # Reproducible relative paths

# ----directory and base imports-------------------------------------------
data_dir <- here("data")  # adjust if needed

# Core IPEDS components
hd  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "HD2023.csv"))  |> clean_names()
adm <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "ADM2023.csv")) |> clean_names()
om  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "OM2023.csv"))  |> clean_names()

# Finance (public / private nonprofit / private for-profit)
f1a <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F1A.csv")) |> clean_names()
f2  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F2.csv"))  |> clean_names()
f3  <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "F2223_F3.csv"))  |> clean_names()

# 12-month instructional activity (FTE source)
efia <- read_csv(file.path(data_dir, "EFIA2023.csv")) |> clean_names()

# ----build FTE from EFIA2023----------------------------------------------
efia_fte <- efia |>
  mutate(across(c(fteug, efteug, ftegd, eftegd, ftedpp),
                ~ readr::parse_number(as.character(.)))) |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    fte_ug    = coalesce(fteug, efteug),
    fte_grad  = coalesce(ftegd, eftegd),
    fte_dpp   = ftedpp,
    fte_total = coalesce(fteug, efteug, 0) +
                coalesce(ftegd, eftegd, 0) +
                coalesce(ftedpp, 0)
  )

# ----align finance variables across control types-------------------------
f1a_fin <- f1a |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f1d01,   # Total revenues & other additions (public)
    instr_exp = f1c011,  # Instruction - current year total
    tot_exp   = f1n07,   # Total expenses
    control   = "Public"
  )

f2_fin <- f2 |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f2d162,  # Total revenues & investment return - unrestricted
    instr_exp = f2e011,  # Instruction - total amount
    tot_exp   = f2b02,   # Total expenses
    control   = "Private Nonprofit"
  )

f3_fin <- f3 |>
  transmute(
    unitid,
    tot_rev   = f3d12,   # Total revenues & investment return
    instr_exp = f3e011,  # Instruction - total amount
    tot_exp   = f3b02,   # Total expenses
    control   = "Private For-Profit"
  )

fin <- bind_rows(f1a_fin, f2_fin, f3_fin)

# ----merge all components--------------------------------------------------
ipeds <- hd |>
  left_join(efia_fte, by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(fin,      by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(adm,      by = "unitid") |>
  left_join(om,       by = "unitid") |>
  filter(!is.na(unitid), !is.na(fte_total), fte_total > 0) |>
  distinct(unitid, .keep_all = TRUE) |>
  mutate(
    rev_per_fte    = tot_rev   / fte_total,
    instr_exp_fte  = instr_exp / fte_total,
    exp_per_fte    = tot_exp   / fte_total
  )

title: Capstone: K-Means Clustering on Retail Data
text:
In retail, not all customers are the same. Some shop often and spend a lot, while others buy less or shop only occasionally. Treating all customers the same can lead to missed opportunities. K-Means clustering helps retailers by grouping customers with similar behaviors, such as spending levels or shopping frequency. These groups can then be targeted with the right offers, discounts, and services. Beyond customers, K-Means can also be used in inventory management, dividing products into fast-moving, stable, or slow-moving categories to reduce waste and improve stock planning.
For this project we are working with a retail dataset that holds transactional records with details on purchases and spending patterns. Our plan is to clean and prepare the data, choose features that capture customer and product behavior, and then apply K-Means clustering to see how the groups form. From there we will evaluate the clusters and describe them in clear terms, showing how the results can guide decisions for marketing, promotions, and inventory.

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Literature Review


Source Summaries (click to expand)


Cluster Analysis in Higher Education Research
PDF Link – Springer
The chapter reviews how cluster analysis is used to study diversity and structure among higher education institutions. The authors explain how statistical grouping exposes institutional similarities that typical classification systems overlook. They discuss the method’s flexibility for understanding performance and policy patterns across universities and show how it can support empirical research on institutional behavior.

Institutional Groupings in IPEDS: Considerations for Data Use
Web Link – NCES
This NCES publication outlines the logic and procedures for creating institutional groupings using standardized IPEDS variables. It focuses on the need for consistency, variable alignment, and transparency when comparing data across schools. The document highlights how structured variable relationships can support reproducible and fair institutional comparisons across the national education system.

Identification of Student Behavioral Patterns in Higher Education Using K-Means Clustering and Support Vector Machine
PDF Link – MDPI Applied Sciences
The study applies K-Means clustering to student behavior and performance data, validating results with a Support Vector Machine. The authors used normalized features, centroid checks, and cluster validation to identify three distinct learning behavior groups. They found that clustering helped simplify large datasets into actionable patterns, showing how unsupervised models can classify educational behavior at scale.

Proposal of a New Method to Classify Higher Education Institutions
PDF Link – Otterbein University Digital Commons
This thesis introduces a two-step method that combines factor analysis and cluster analysis to build a new classification of universities. The author selected academic, financial, and demographic indicators to find groupings that better represent institutional diversity. The results show that data-driven group formation can outperform fixed classification systems and highlight how numerical traits can define institutional identity.

A Hybrid Approach to Identifying National Peer Institutions
PDF Link – Texas Association for Institutional Research (TAIR)
This report explains how statistical clustering and expert review can be combined to identify peer institutions. Quantitative results were first generated from performance and enrollment data, then refined through institutional judgment to improve interpretability. The authors conclude that pairing data models with professional context leads to more balanced and credible peer comparisons.

Merging Data to Facilitate Analyses
PDF Link – Robert Kelchen
Kelchen describes the process of joining and cleaning educational data for large-scale analysis. The guide details how to handle schema differences, missing values, and inconsistent labels across datasets like IPEDS and federal records. It stresses the importance of reproducibility and documentation when merging data sources to maintain accuracy in quantitative research.

title: Data-Driven Segmentation of U.S. Colleges and Universities Using K-Means Clustering on IPEDS Data
text:
Data Description and Visualization

Dataset Overview
This study uses institutional-level data from the Integrated Postsecondary Education Data System (IPEDS) for the 2023 collection year (2023–2024 academic cycle), maintained by the National Center for Education Statistics (NCES). IPEDS collects standardized information from all U.S. postsecondary institutions participating in federal financial aid programs. The combined dataset provides national coverage across all control types—public, private nonprofit, and private for-profit—allowing for a comprehensive clustering analysis of institutional characteristics.
The following survey components were used and merged using the common key UNITID:

HD2023: Institutional Characteristics (general info, state, sector, control type, FTE enrollment)

F2223_F1A: Finance – Public institutions (GASB format)

F2223_F2: Finance – Private nonprofit institutions (FASB format)

F2223_F3: Finance – Private for-profit institutions (optional inclusion for completeness)

ADM2023: Admissions (admission rate, SAT/ACT averages, tuition and fees)

OM2023: Outcome Measures (student completion and success rates)

All data files were downloaded directly from the NCES IPEDS Data Center. The merge was performed by UNITID, and institutions without valid identifiers or enrollment data were excluded to ensure comparability across survey components.



Variable Selection and Preparation
To capture the main dimensions of institutional performance and scale, the following variables were selected:







Conceptual Domain
Example Variables (Field Names)




Institutional Scale
ugds (undergraduate enrollment), fte (full-time equivalent), student_faculty_ratio


Financial Resources
f1a02 / f2a02 (total revenues), f1a13 / f2a13 (instructional expenses), derived ratios: revenue_per_fte, instruction_exp_per_fte


Access and Aid
admrate (admission rate), tuition1 (in-state tuition), %pell (Pell Grant recipients)


Outcomes
om2_pct_comp (completion rate), gradrate (graduation rate), retention_rate



All numeric variables were standardized using z-score normalization to ensure comparability in K-Means clustering. Outliers were capped at the 1st and 99th percentiles using Winsorization to reduce distortion of centroids.



Data Cleaning and Integration
Public (F1A) and private (F2) finance datasets were vertically merged using consistent variable naming conventions. For each institution, financial data were joined to demographic and admissions information. Missing values for financial variables were replaced with NA rather than imputation, to maintain integrity of original reporting. The merged file included approximately 6,000 active, degree-granting institutions after filtering.
